solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: End of the dire PM — ruined lives — a superficial thing

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word 'the'

indicators.note: something ruined has been wrecked, so the words before it are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
to live is to be, so 'lives' can mean 'is'

explanation.surface: A gloomy jibe that a dreadful Prime Minister wrecks lives and is all surface with no depth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lives' gives IS in the sense 'exists'; EPIDERMIS is read literally as a superficial thing.
explanation.definitionFit: The epidermis is the outer layer of skin, literally a thing lying on the surface of the body.

clue.text: Evans, having been dehospitalised, is a disaster

indicators.note: taking the hospital out of someone means dropping the map abbreviation for a hospital from the name

parts.note: Chris Evans, the British radio and TV presenter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A celebrity just discharged from hospital is in a bad way.
explanation.walkthrough: H is the standard abbreviation for hospital (as on road signs), so removing it from CHRIS leaves CRIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisis is a moment of acute trouble or danger, a near synonym for a disaster.

clue.text: Bang Lola stupid? Not an earthly!

indicators.note: something stupid is muddled or senseless, so the letters are jumbled
'not' tells the solver these letters are absent from the mix

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
the letters to be taken away from the mix

explanation.surface: Someone asks if Lola is stupid and gets the slangy reply 'not an earthly', meaning not a chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not an earthly' is a British idiom for 'no chance at all', which hides the definition at the very end.
explanation.definitionFit: Global means relating to the whole world, so it can stand in for earthly as an adjective.

clue.text: Dodgy football side hides debt

indicators.note: to hide something is to keep it inside, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: Spurs is the nickname of Tottenham Hotspur, a London football club
an IOU is a written acknowledgement of a debt

explanation.surface: A football club with shady accounts conceals what it owes.
explanation.definitionFit: Spurious means false or not genuine, which matches the informal sense of dodgy as untrustworthy.

clue.text: Blustering politicians 8dn often are wanting everyone to be a peer with roll

parts.note: all means everyone
read as 'pee-er', one who pees; to piss is to be one
and means together with
to roll something up is to wind it

explanation.surface: Campaigning politicians all longing for a seat in the House of Lords along with the trappings.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is reading 'peer' (a lord) as someone who pees. 8dn points to ELECTIONEERING, the answer to 8-down.
explanation.definitionFit: 'All piss and wind' is a crude British idiom for someone full of empty talk and bluster, as campaigning politicians often are.

clue.text: A titled person matters if secreting drugs

indicators.note: to secrete is to hide away, so one piece is tucked inside another

parts.note: something that matters counts
E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, plural Es

explanation.surface: A complaint that being titled is only important if you are hiding drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A countess is the wife of an earl or count, or holds that rank herself, so she bears a noble title.

clue.text: Standard fancy woman of Charles, the Irish leader

parts.note: par is the standard or norm
Nell Gwyn was the mistress of King Charles II

explanation.surface: Reads like gossip about the usual mistress of a man called Charles, who led the Irish.
explanation.walkthrough: The Charles in the clue points two ways: Charles II, whose mistress was Nell Gwyn, and Charles Stewart Parnell, whose own affair with Kitty O'Shea ruined him.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Stewart Parnell led the Irish Parliamentary Party and the Home Rule movement in the 1880s.

clue.text: One gin and erectile dysfunction — it's coming to its climax

indicators.note: a dysfunction is a failure to work properly, so the letters fall out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of a drink and impotence on the way to the bedroom finale.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'climax' is innocently the run-up to polling day, when campaigning peaks.
explanation.definitionFit: Electioneering is campaigning, which builds to its peak as the vote approaches.

clue.text: Pope's contraception advice in magazine section?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: withdrawal, the only method the Catholic church tolerates short of abstinence, crudely put
second meaning: a detachable supplement inside a magazine

explanation.walkthrough: The Catholic church forbids artificial contraception, so the joke is that withdrawal is the Pope's advice.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both the imperative 'withdraw' and the noun for a removable section of a publication.

clue.text: see 24dn.
Insult MP, Butcher

parts.note: to dis is slang for to insult
an MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A short headline: someone insults an MP named Butcher.
explanation.walkthrough: Butcher looks like a surname, but it is a verb meaning cut up.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismember is to cut off the limbs, as a butcher carves a carcass.

clue.text: Member Enclosure 1, Sandown's first

parts.note: a pen is an enclosure for animals
the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of Sandown

explanation.surface: Reads like a racecourse signpost: the members' enclosure number one at Sandown Park.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandown Park is an English racecourse, and racecourses have a Members' Enclosure; the capitalised 'Member' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Member is a familiar euphemism for the male organ.

clue.text: Dotty tries to engage once more in parliamentary business

definitions.text: engage once more in parliamentary business

indicators.note: dotty means crazy, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An eccentric attempts to get back into the work of Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: Parliament 'sits' when in session, so to sit again is to engage once more in its business.
explanation.definitionFit: To resit is to sit again, and a sitting is the period when Parliament conducts business.

clue.text: Ladies possibly seek kinky gander

parts.note: the Ladies is a public toilet, a loo; 'possibly' marks it as one example

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the word before it is bent out of order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Women looking for a pervy male goose.
explanation.walkthrough: Gander looks like the male goose; it is informal British for a quick look.
explanation.definitionFit: A look-see is a quick inspection, and 'have a gander' is British slang for having a look.

clue.text: No problem getting 'ayes' to vacillate, vegetable-like?

indicators.note: to vacillate is to waver back and forth, so the letters shift about

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
like a pea, the vegetable

explanation.surface: An easy vote in the Commons where wavering yes votes are oddly like greens.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy-peasy is a childish British phrase for very easy, just as 'no problem' signals a simple task.

clue.text: Briefly part of the clique, no friend of Blair

parts.note: to be in is to belong to the favoured group
Clare Short, the Labour cabinet minister who resigned over Tony Blair's Iraq war

explanation.surface: Someone briefly part of the inner circle who fell out with Tony Blair.
explanation.walkthrough: Clare Short was International Development Secretary and became a fierce critic of Blair after resigning in 2003.
explanation.definitionFit: 'In short' means to put it briefly, an adverbial phrase like 'briefly'.

clue.text: Quality of 'misery memoirs' makes you spit ("life I traded for agony finally")

indicators.note: to make something out of material is to form a new shape, so the letters are rebuilt in a fresh order
a thing traded for another is swapped out, so one letter is exchanged for a different one

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
the letter to be swapped out of the second word
the final letter of agony

explanation.surface: A gibe that miserable memoirs make readers spit, the author having swapped a life for wallowing in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: Replace the I in LIFE with Y to get LYFE, then rearrange it with SPIT. 'Misery memoirs' are a genre of tell-all books about abusive childhoods.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-pity is wallowing in one's own sorrows, the defining mood of the misery memoir genre.

clue.text: The one mentioned by Blair — i.e. lacking as a has-been PM

parts.note: that points to the one already referred to

indicators.note: lacking means going without, so the letters named just before are taken out

parts.note: Cherie Blair, Tony Blair's wife
the letters to be dropped

explanation.surface: Tony Blair mentions a predecessor who is now out of power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blair' looks like Tony but means his wife Cherie; dropping I and E from her name leaves CHER.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret Thatcher was Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990, so by the time of this clue a former PM.

clue.text: City of sawn-off shotguns, initially half each

indicators.note: sawn-off suggests something cut and disordered, so 'off' signals the letters going awry
taking half of a word means losing the rest, here keeping the front portion

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of shotguns
taken as written, then cut in half

explanation.surface: A city's gangsters each get half the sawn-off shotguns.
explanation.definitionFit: Swansea is a coastal city in south Wales.

clue.text: Apply tongue all over retiring ex-President of USA and take a rest

indicators.note: something all over another covers it on every side, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: to lick is to apply the tongue

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the name is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: Abe Lincoln, sixteenth US President

explanation.surface: A lurid image of licking a former US President before having a lie-down.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie back is to recline and relax, which is taking a rest.

clue.text: Kelvin on NASA's "liberal" state

parts.note: K is the symbol for kelvin, the unit of temperature

indicators.note: a liberal treatment is a free one, so the letters are freely rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone called Kelvin comments on the space agency being 'liberal' about the state.
explanation.definitionFit: Kansas is one of the fifty US states, in the Midwest.

clue.text: Hairy pair of investigators getting their ends away

indicators.note: with their ends taken away, each word loses its last letter; the phrase is also slang for having sex

parts.note: two slang words for a detective: dick and (private) eye

explanation.surface: Two detectives, one hirsute, having sex, in British slang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting your end away' is British slang for having sex; here it simply drops each word's last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Hairy is informal British for risky or frightening, the same as dicey.

clue.text: Brian and his mater's alcoholic successor

parts.note: Private Eye calls Prince Charles 'Brian'; Chas is short for Charles
his mother is the Queen, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: Reads like a remark about a family's heir with a drink problem.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye nicknames the Queen 'Brenda' and Prince Charles 'Brian'; mater is old school slang for mother.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaser is a drink taken straight after another, such as beer after a shot of spirits.

clue.text: (& 10dn.) Searching examination makes one drunk cite "DTs"

parts.note: a means one

indicators.note: a drunk person is unsteady and confused, so the letters reel into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A tough test that leaves someone so drunk they claim delirium tremens.
explanation.walkthrough: DTs are delirium tremens, the shakes from alcohol withdrawal, which fits the drunk surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An acid test is a decisive trial of worth, originally nitric acid used to test gold.

clue.text: Skip gives head to Brenda

parts.note: a cap is the top or head of something
Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A boat's skipper offers oral sex to a woman named Brenda.
explanation.walkthrough: Skip looks like a captain; it is a verb for a frisky jump.
explanation.definitionFit: To caper is to skip or dance about playfully.

clue.text: Frank scoffed as one who'll be 8dn

parts.note: frank means candid
to scoff is to eat greedily

explanation.surface: Someone called Frank mocked a would-be campaigner.
explanation.walkthrough: 8dn is ELECTIONEERING, the answer to 8-down. Scoffed looks like 'mocked'; it is British slang for ate.
explanation.definitionFit: A candidate standing for office will spend the run-up to polling day campaigning for votes.

clue.text: Feature of bidet: enteritis tension relaxer

indicators.note: a feature of something is part of it, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A bidet as a soothing remedy for inflamed bowels.
explanation.definitionFit: Détente is an easing of hostility between nations, a relaxing of political tension.

clue.text: Cameron's second day shift, an 8dn speech?

indicators.note: the second of a word is its letter in position two, so just that one is kept

parts.note: the letter in second place in Cameron
the standard abbreviation for day
a shift is a simple straight dress

explanation.surface: David Cameron's second day at work, delivering a campaign speech.
explanation.walkthrough: Shift looks like a work period; it is a loose dress. 8dn is ELECTIONEERING.
